title: Recording tuba and whistles for Springsteen's Seeger Sessions
summary: He describes being called to overdub tuba and whistles at Springsteen's studio and a follow-up session.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Didn’t you recently do something with Bruce Springsteen also?

That was another one of those gigs like out of the blue. So you don’t sit around thinking oh man I wish I had a gig with Bruce Springsteen because you know he says his E Street Band and he has regular horns. Like the guys who are on Conan O’Brien, Mark Pender and La Bamba the trombone player, Richie, they play with him a lot. Well some friends of mine had been playing with him for years. On his birthdays they would play his parties, called the Golfing Playboys, and like did Zydeco and stuff like that and the drummer’s, a great drummer, could play the rub board and all kinds of beats, and named Larry Eagle. So they’d been doing this for years, and then Bruce got called to do some numbers on a CD to — what’s the word I’m looking for — to just to honor Pete Seeger. And so he used that band. He recorded that band. Like “We Shall Overcome,” and something, he recorded a bunch with them. I think “We Shall Overcome” ended up on the CD. And after recording them, he recorded them again and it was a many year project. And then he started really getting into the idea of finishing the CD, whether he put it out or not. So when he was finishing it, I mean everything was live with these people. And many things happened that I don’t know exactly. And then he said, “I want to put a tuba in here and some pennywhistle, because he was doing some Irish stuff too. So they were saying, “You guys know a good tuba player for this?” and they gave them some names, and then the pennywhistle, and the drummer said, “Wait a minute, I’ve got a friend who plays both. The funny thing is I’d only played trombone with him, but I think he remembered seeing it in my car. But he said he knew I played them well. So I got the call just to do one recording on top of this wonderful — you know usually — you know, you’re a sax player, did you ever do a thing where you’re overdubbing on a track?

You know and sometimes it’s fun and sometimes like where’s the beat. Plus playing tuba, it’s like a bass thing. So if it’s not in there, and I really had to hear what the bass player was doing. It was so easy. I’m in a recording studio, they sent a limo to my house in New York to go to South Jersey to Rumson where one of his houses was where he had a recording studio there. So they’re doing this stuff and I’m listening to all this music. They’re doing a little editing before I come in. And I’m like sitting there thinking what is this going to be like and I hadn’t met Bruce yet, I don’t think so, I think I met the engineer, a really great guy, Toby. And I’m thinking what’s this going to be like. So I’m warming up. I had two tubas with me, I had a small E flat and a bigger B flat. And I’ve got all these whistles with me with the different keys. And I want to make sure, you know, I’m a little nervous. It’s rare at this point in my life that there is someone where I © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-

could be like oh I’m playing with so-and so, you know, like that. And so it took a while for him to get ready. They keep the limo there, they’re paying for the limo, and I’m talking about a really nice limo. “Would you like a drink or something?” Stuff like that. And so I’m listening to them do the music and they’re doing a little editing they had to finish, and it was all stuff I knew from playing in that jug band.

So I go wow, this is going to be great. Even later on I said, “Hey, you want to hear the jug too?” So he had me come in and he just wanted the tuba in some spots, and it was funny, like I’m a really good reader, and he had a — not a super hard whistle part, but just give me some time to learn it. Often I’ll say like give me a few minutes and let me write it down, so take after take I’ll know exactly what the notes are supposed to be instead of trying to remember. But we didn’t do it that way. But the whistle stuff went fine, the tuba went fine. He was cool, man, he was great man, and like in the middle of the session the phone rings and they said, “Hey Bruce, it’s Patti,” you know, his wife. “Are you going to pick up the kids at school today?” And he was great. And he shook my hand. And it’s funny, you know the trombone is my major instrument, and so I know when I’m playing well on trombone and when it’s being rolled to tape or to the hard drive, but you know you don’t know a hundred percent sure. We ended up using the smaller tuba and a bunch of whistles, and I thought I did okay but then again you never know. You never know if someone’s going to go like okay it was a mistake, we shouldn’t have booked it. Or you never know, oh we really loved it. You never know what’s happening. So I got a call about ten days later, he we want to do another session. So I guess he liked me.

So I went down there and during the session this other guy was there, George, one of the managers. And someone told me, he says, “We’re thinking about maybe doing a couple of gigs with this band.” When I first went in there they didn’t even know if they were going to release this. It became “The Seeger Sessions” the record that came out.
